stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
stimulus:
The following text is adapted from Marisol Ekwueme's 2019 novel The Long Rows. Ines, an agricultural researcher, is visiting her test fields after a summer without rain.

Ines had driven out expecting to find nothing. The neighboring farms were brown to the fence line, their corn folded over like paper. But at the edge of her plots she stopped. The wheat she had spent six years crossing and recrossing stood upright, thin but green, its heads already filling. She knelt and pressed a stalk between her fingers, as if to be sure it was real, and found that she was laughing.
choices: Ines is relieved to discover that the wheat she developed has survived the drought.
Ines is discouraged to find that her test plots fared no better than nearby farms.
Ines worries that her neighbors will resent the success of her experimental crop.
Ines notices that the corn on neighboring farms has been damaged by the dry summer.
explanation: You follow Ines from expecting to find nothing to kneeling in disbelief and laughing. The turn at 'But' shows her wheat has survived when everything around it died, and her laughter shows relief and joy. Choice A matches both the situation and that emotional direction.

B.why: You reversed the tone. Ines expected failure, but the text says her wheat 'stood upright' and green while the nearby farms were brown. Her laughing shows the opposite of discouragement.

C.why: You added a motive the text never gives. Nothing suggests Ines is thinking about her neighbors' feelings. Their farms appear only as a contrast to her surviving wheat.

D.why: You picked a true detail from the second sentence, but it is too narrow. The dead corn is background that sets up the real focus: Ines's reaction to her own wheat.

subtype_name: Main idea of a fiction or poetry excerpt
license: CC BY 4.0 - original item, not College Board content
rated_why: clear contrast shown: expected nothing, found success; one direct emotional meaning

stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
stimulus:
The following text is from Tomasz Reyna's 2008 poem "Proof." The speaker is a printmaker.

All morning I cut the block by feel,
gouging the pale wood toward a shape
I carried backward in my head.
I rolled the ink, black and slow as tar,
laid the paper, leaned my weight on it.
Only when I peeled the sheet away
did I see what my hands had meant—
the heron, facing the right way at last,
more certain than I ever was.
choices: The speaker describes the tools and materials needed to cut and ink a woodblock.
The speaker is frustrated that the finished print differs from the image planned.
The speaker works without fully seeing the image until the finished print reveals it.
The speaker regrets choosing a medium that offers so little certainty to the artist.
explanation: In plain English: the speaker carves 'by feel' with the image held 'backward' in mind, and 'only when' the paper comes off does the heron appear clearly, 'more certain' than the speaker felt. The poem moves from working half-blind to seeing the image revealed, and choice C covers both parts.

A.why: You described only the images from the first lines (the block, the ink, the paper) and missed the turn at 'Only when,' where the poem arrives at its point.

B.why: You reversed the tone. The heron faces 'the right way at last.' The print shows what the speaker's hands 'had meant,' so it matches the speaker's intention rather than disappointing it.

D.why: You added a regret the poem never states. The speaker admits to uncertainty but never wishes for a different medium. The ending sounds like wonder, not regret.

subtype_name: Main idea of a fiction or poetry excerpt
license: CC BY 4.0 - original item, not College Board content
rated_why: simple structure: work blindly, then see result; main idea is obvious from the poem's final moment

stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
stimulus:
The following text is adapted from Harriet Olumide's 2015 novel Census. Theo, a graduate student in ornithology, is conducting a morning bird count in a marsh.

Theo had been told the count would be tedious: three hours on a wet platform, tallying whatever flew past. By the first hour he had filled two pages. A pair of rails picked through the reeds below him; a harrier swung low over the water and was gone. He forgot the cold in his boots. When his supervisor's truck pulled up, Theo looked at his watch in disbelief. It seemed impossible that the morning was already over.
choices: Theo finds the bird count just as tedious as others had warned him it would be.
Theo becomes so absorbed in the bird count that the morning passes unnoticed.
Theo hopes to impress his supervisor by recording more birds than expected.
Theo watches a harrier fly low over the marsh water before it disappears.
explanation: Theo was warned the count would be tedious, but he fills pages, forgets the cold, and can't believe the morning is over. Those are signs of someone absorbed in his work, and choice B captures that.

A.why: You took the warning in the first sentence as Theo's real experience. Everything after it, such as forgetting the cold and his 'disbelief' at the time, shows the count was the opposite of tedious.

C.why: You added a motive the text never gives. The supervisor shows up only to mark the end of the morning. Nothing says Theo is trying to impress anyone.

D.why: You chose one image from the middle of the passage. The harrier is one of many sights that hold Theo's attention, not the point of the passage.

subtype_name: Main idea of a fiction or poetry excerpt
license: CC BY 4.0 - original item, not College Board content
rated_why: straightforward contrast between expectation (tedium) and reality (absorbed); time markers make the shift unmistakable

stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
stimulus:
The following text is adapted from Ansel Varga's 2021 novel Contour Lines. Lucía, a cartographer, is preparing a new map of the valley where she grew up.

Lucía had drawn hundreds of valleys, but never her own. The survey data arrived on a Tuesday, and she traced it as she would any other: the ridgeline, the river, the new reservoir spreading blue across the lower fields. Only when she began to letter the names did she pause. There was no label to give the square where her grandmother had kept goats, no road to mark to the schoolhouse. The water covered all of it. She set down her pen and did not pick it up again until evening.
choices: Lucía is pleased to finally have the chance to map the valley where she grew up.
Lucía leaves the flooded village off the map to avoid upsetting her own family.
Lucía uses survey data to trace the ridgeline and river of a mountain valley.
Lucía is saddened when mapping her home valley shows that familiar places are gone.
explanation: Lucía starts out treating the job like any other, then stops when she sees that the places she remembers are under the reservoir. Putting down her pen until evening shows her grief. Choice D matches both the situation and the move toward loss.

A.why: You reversed the tone. The text never shows Lucía pleased. It builds toward her stopping work entirely because of what the water has covered.

B.why: You added a motive and an action the text never gives. The places are missing from the map because they are underwater, not because Lucía chose to hide them from anyone.

C.why: You chose a true description of the routine part of the passage and missed the pause that follows, which is where the passage's meaning lies.

subtype_name: Main idea of a fiction or poetry excerpt
license: CC BY 4.0 - original item, not College Board content
rated_why: clear emotional moment when familiar places are gone; sadness is shown directly through the pause and setting down pen

stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
stimulus:
The following text is from Noor Castellanos's 2017 poem "Gauge." The speaker is a hydrologist who measures a river's height each spring.

Each spring I wade out to the gauge
and read the river by its rising marks,
the numbers climbing inch by inch
with snow that fell on peaks I'll never climb.
I write them down. I send them on.
But this year, standing waist-deep in the cold,
I felt the whole weight of the mountain's winter
pressing past my legs toward the sea,
and then, and only then, I understood
what all my columns had been counting.
choices: The speaker explains the procedure for recording a river's height every spring.
The speaker realizes, while doing a routine task, the force behind the numbers.
The speaker grows tired of measuring a river whose changes seem too small.
The speaker gives up recording data in favor of experiencing the river directly.
explanation: In plain English: every year the speaker reads the gauge and passes along the numbers, but this year, feeling the snowmelt push past, the speaker 'then, and only then' understands what those numbers stand for. Choice B includes both the routine and the realization it leads to.

A.why: You described only the first five lines, the routine of reading and recording, and missed the turn at 'But this year' that leads to the speaker's realization.

C.why: You reversed the tone. The speaker feels 'the whole weight' of the river, not changes too small to matter, and the poem ends in understanding rather than weariness.

D.why: You added a decision the poem never states. The speaker comes to understand the columns of data. Nothing says the speaker stops keeping them.

subtype_name: Main idea of a fiction or poetry excerpt
license: CC BY 4.0 - original item, not College Board content
rated_why: moment-of-realization structure is explicit; shift from routine to understanding is clearly marked

stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
stimulus:
The following text is adapted from Desmond Achterberg's 2012 novel Load Paths. Walter, a retired civil engineer, is being driven across a bridge he helped design forty years earlier.

His granddaughter drove, chatting about her classes, and Walter let her talk. As the car climbed onto the span, he felt the old habit return: he listened for the joints, watched the cables, counted the lamp posts. Every one was where he had put it. Traffic streamed past in both directions, hundreds of people who had never heard his name and never needed to. Walter settled back in his seat and smiled. Forty years, and it was still holding everyone up.
choices: Walter feels quiet pride that the bridge he designed still serves people so well.
Walter is anxious that the aging bridge may no longer be safe for drivers to cross.
Walter is hurt that the people crossing his bridge do not know who designed it.
Walter's granddaughter talks to him about her classes while she drives the car.
explanation: Walter checks the bridge out of old habit, finds everything where he put it, then settles back and smiles because it is 'still holding everyone up.' That is quiet pride in lasting work, which is choice A.

B.why: You read his listening and watching as worry. The text calls it 'the old habit,' and what he finds, every part where he put it, leads him to relax and smile rather than feel anxious.

C.why: You added a hurt feeling the text never gives. The drivers 'never needed to' know his name, and Walter smiles right after, so he is content, not wounded.

D.why: You chose a background detail from the first sentence. The granddaughter's chatter sets the scene, but the passage is about Walter's feelings toward the bridge.

subtype_name: Main idea of a fiction or poetry excerpt
license: CC BY 4.0 - original item, not College Board content
rated_why: main idea (quiet pride in lasting work) shown through checking actions and final smile; distractors easily ruled out

stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
stimulus:
The following text is adapted from Leela Arnaud's 2020 novel The Field Reels. Priya, a musicologist, is cataloging old field recordings in a university archive.

The reel was labeled only with a date and the name of a village. Priya threaded it onto the machine as she had threaded two hundred others that month, pencil ready for the catalog card. A woman's voice came through the hiss, unaccompanied, singing low. Priya's pencil stopped. She knew the tune before she knew why: it was the song her mother had hummed over the washing, the one Priya had never heard anywhere else. She played it three times before she wrote a single word.
choices: Priya grows impatient with the slow, repetitive work of cataloging recordings.
Priya suspects that the reel was mislabeled and belongs to a different village.
Priya threads a reel onto the machine and prepares to fill out a catalog card.
Priya is deeply moved to recognize a song from her childhood in a recording.
explanation: Priya starts the reel as routine work, then her pencil stops when she recognizes her mother's song. Playing it three times before writing anything shows how moved she is. Choice D covers both the discovery and her feeling about it.

A.why: You fixed on 'two hundred others' and assumed boredom. The passage turns away from routine at the moment she hears the song, and she lingers over the recording instead of rushing through it.

B.why: You added a suspicion the text never gives. The sparse label is simply how the reel arrives. Priya's reaction is recognition, not doubt about where it came from.

C.why: You described only the setup in the first two sentences and missed the moment of recognition that the rest of the passage builds toward.

subtype_name: Main idea of a fiction or poetry excerpt
license: CC BY 4.0 - original item, not College Board content
rated_why: clear trigger (recognizing childhood song) and emotional reaction (stops, plays three times); personal connection is unmistakable

stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
stimulus:
The following text is adapted from Rafael Okonkwo-Hale's 2018 novel Right of Way. Elena, a city planner, is walking through a neighborhood shaped by a road project she approved years earlier.

On the drawings, the expressway had been a clean gray line, and Elena had been proud of how neatly it bypassed downtown. Walking beneath it now, she saw what the drawings had left out. The corner bakery was gone; so was the street that had led to it. Children cut through a chain-link gap to reach a school that had once been two blocks away. Elena had signed off on every page. She stood under the roar of traffic and wished, not for the first time, that she had looked harder.
choices: Elena is proud that the expressway she approved bypasses downtown so neatly.
Elena plans to propose removing the expressway at the next council meeting.
Elena regrets not foreseeing how the road she approved would harm a neighborhood.
Elena notices that children use a gap in a fence to reach their nearby school.
explanation: Elena's pride belongs to the past ('had been proud'). Walking under the expressway now, she sees what it destroyed and 'wished... that she had looked harder.' The passage moves from past pride to present regret, which is choice C.

A.why: You stopped at the first sentence. Her pride is in the past tense, and the rest of the passage replaces it with regret. The word 'wished' at the end tells you how she feels now.

B.why: You added a plan the text never mentions. Elena wishes she had acted differently in the past. Nothing says she intends to do anything at a council meeting.

D.why: You chose one true detail from the middle. The children cutting through the fence is one piece of evidence of harm, not the idea the whole passage is about.

subtype_name: Main idea of a fiction or poetry excerpt
license: CC BY 4.0 - original item, not College Board content
rated_why: stark contrast between clean drawing and destructive reality; regret is shown through specific lost places and her wish

stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
stimulus:
The following text is adapted from a novel. Ruth, a nurse, has spent the day running a free vaccination clinic in her town's small library.

At nine that morning, Ruth had counted the folding chairs and wondered who would ever sit in them. By noon the line reached past the card catalog. Farmers came in work boots, mothers carried toddlers on their hips, and one old man announced he hadn't seen a needle since the army. Now, packing the empty vials into their box, Ruth noticed she was humming. She had not expected the town to come, and it had.
choices: Ruth is pleased that the clinic drew far more people than she had expected.
Ruth is worried that the clinic will run out of vaccine before the line ends.
Ruth is amused that an old man at the clinic had once served in the army.
Ruth is relieved that the clinic let her avoid a difficult shift at the hospital.
explanation: Follow Ruth from start to finish. In the morning she doubts anyone will fill the chairs. By noon the line is long, and by the end she is humming and thinking that the town came when she 'had not expected' it to. The last sentence sums up the feeling the details build toward: she is pleased by a turnout that beat her expectations. Choice A gets both the situation and that direction right.

B.why: You flipped the tone. Ruth does worry, but only at the start and only about nobody coming. By the end she is humming over empty vials, and nothing suggests she fears running short.

C.why: You chose a choice that is too narrow. The old man is one example in a list of people who came. He supports the main point, which is how big the turnout was, but he isn't the point himself.

D.why: You gave Ruth a motive the text never mentions. The passage says nothing about the hospital or about her wanting to avoid any work. Her feeling comes from the town showing up.

stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
stimulus:
The following text is from a poem. The speaker is looking at a distant star through a backyard telescope.

A white point, steady over the garden wall,
cold as a nail-head in the dark.
I learned tonight its light set out
before my grandmother was born.
So what I hold here in the glass
is not the star, but a letter from it,
and I stand reading it long after
the sender may have gone.
choices: The speaker reflects that the starlight is so old that the star may no longer exist.
The speaker describes how bright and cold the star looks above the garden wall.
The speaker is disappointed that the telescope shows the star as only a small point.
The speaker regrets never having shown this particular star to a beloved grandmother.
explanation: Start by putting the whole poem into plain English. The first two lines describe the star. Then the speaker learns that its light left the star generations ago, and the poem turns on 'So': what the speaker sees is only a 'letter' from the star, and the star itself 'may have gone.' The main idea is that reflection about old light and a star that may no longer be there.

B.why: You stopped at the opening images. The first two lines do describe a bright, cold point of light, but the poem moves past them to a reflection about the age of that light, and this choice leaves the turn out.

C.why: You read the wrong tone. The speaker calls the star a small 'white point' but is not let down by it. The speaker stands there absorbed, 'reading' the light like a letter.

D.why: You added a regret the poem doesn't include. The grandmother appears only to show how long ago the light left the star. The speaker never says anything about wanting to share the star with her.
